title: Play a wine glass its own note loudly enough and the sound can shatter it

cover.alt: Black-and-white high-speed camera views of an intact wine glass standing in front of a loudspeaker, seen from two angles side by side.

body: Tap a wine glass and it rings at its **natural frequency**, the pitch at which it vibrates most easily. A loudspeaker playing exactly that note pushes the rim in step with its own wobble, so every push adds to the last, a build-up called **resonance**. Turn it up enough and the rim flexes further and further until the glass breaks. A note that is off-pitch keeps falling out of step with the glass, so its pushes partly cancel out, which is why the trick needs careful tuning and the right glass.

slides.alt: Two side-by-side black-and-white high-speed views of a wine glass in front of a loudspeaker. The glass trembles for a few seconds, cracks appear, and it bursts into curved shards that fly apart while the stem stays standing.
slides.caption: Two high-speed camera views of the same wine glass: as a loudspeaker plays at it, the glass trembles for a few seconds, then bursts apart.
slides.music: “Evening of Chaos” Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com) · CC BY 4.0

slides.prompt: Every glass breaks at a different note. How can you find the right one for yours?
slides.detail: The ring you hear is its natural frequency, the note it vibrates at most easily. Its size, shape and thickness all affect that pitch, so each glass has its own.

slides.heading: How a note breaks a glass

steps.label: A speaker plays the glass's own note
Each push arrives in step with the rim
The wobble grows with every cycle
The glass flexes past breaking point

left.label: Off-pitch
left.text: The pushes drift in and out of step with the glass's own vibration, so they partly cancel and the rim barely moves.

right.label: On-pitch
right.text: Every push adds to the swing, so the rim flexes further each time until the glass fails.

slides.heading: Can a singer really do it?
slides.text: Yes, though it is hard. In a [2005 episode of MythBusters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MythBusters_%282005_season%29), Adam Savage broke a lead crystal glass with his amplified voice, and then rock singer Jaime Vendera broke one with his unaided voice.

slides.question: What decides which note will shatter a particular glass?
slides.explanation: The note must match the pitch the glass rings at. Loudness matters too, but only once the note is right does each push build on the one before.
